title: Divine omniscience
statement: God knows every true proposition and believes no false proposition.
description: A propositional formulation used here for analysis; it does not by itself settle whether future contingents are presently true.

title: Divine omnipotence
statement: God can actualize every state of affairs whose actualization is metaphysically possible for an agent with perfect power.
description: The qualification excludes pseudo-tasks and leaves open familiar disputes about agent-relative possibility.

title: Essential perfect goodness
statement: God is perfectly good in every metaphysically possible world in which God exists.
description: This is stronger than the claim that God is merely contingently morally perfect.

title: Necessary divine existence
statement: God exists in every metaphysically possible world.
description: This is a modal claim about existence, not an argument that such a being exists.

title: Bivalence for future free acts
statement: Every proposition stating what a creature will freely do has a determinate truth value prior to the act.
description: This concerns semantic or metaphysical determinacy, not whether anyone knows the truth value.

title: Exhaustive definite foreknowledge
statement: God infallibly knows, prior to their occurrence, which future free actions will occur.
description: The temporal wording makes this distinct from atemporal knowledge.

title: Creaturely libertarian freedom
statement: At least some human actions are free, and this freedom is incompatible with those actions being causally determined by prior conditions and laws.
description: This minimal characterization does not decide whether alternative possibilities or sourcehood grounds the freedom.

title: Alternative possibilities requirement
statement: For an action to be free in the relevant libertarian sense, the agent must be able to do otherwise.
description: A restricted principle of alternative possibilities, here applied to creaturely libertarian freedom.

title: Fixity of the past
statement: No agent can now bring it about that the actual past was different.
description: Fatalist arguments require a more precise principle governing which past facts are accidentally necessary; Ockhamist replies distinguish hard and soft facts.

title: Transfer of accidental necessity
statement: If a past fact is now accidentally necessary and it necessarily entails a proposition, that proposition is now accidentally necessary.
description: The scope and validity of transfer principles are disputed, especially when the past fact concerns infallible belief.

title: Divine timelessness
statement: God has no temporal location and does not undergo temporal succession.
description: This is the strong atemporal model of divine eternity.

title: Divine temporality
statement: God exists through temporal succession and has temporally ordered states.
description: Different temporalist views disagree about whether God has always been temporal.

title: Strong divine immutability
statement: God undergoes no intrinsic change.
description: This does not by itself deny changes in relational descriptions of God caused solely by creatures.

title: Strong divine simplicity
statement: God has no metaphysical parts or intrinsic composition, and God is not really distinct from the divine intrinsic attributes.
description: This captures a strong classical doctrine rather than every weaker use of “simplicity.”

title: Contingency of this creation
statement: There is a metaphysically possible world in which God exists but does not create this total created order.
description: This does not require that God could create nothing at all, only that this total order is not necessary.

title: Divine creative freedom
statement: God’s decision whether and what to create is free.
description: This deliberately leaves the relevant analysis of divine freedom open.

title: Alternatives required for divine freedom
statement: God’s creative choice is free only if God could have chosen otherwise.
description: This is an incompatibilist analysis of divine freedom and is not assumed by the general claim that God creates freely.

title: Prevolitional middle knowledge
statement: Prior in explanatory order to the creative decree, God knows the true counterfactuals of libertarian creaturely freedom.
description: The priority is logical or explanatory rather than necessarily temporal.

title: Theological determination
statement: God’s creative decree causally determines every human action.
description: This is stronger than meticulous providence if the latter is understood without causal determination.

title: Open future contingents
statement: Some propositions about future free creaturely actions are not yet determinately true or false.
description: This semantic/metaphysical claim is one route to open theism but does not by itself constitute a full doctrine of providence.
